(650 - 1168 AD) The archaeological zone of Huapalcalco is located in Tulancingo de Bravo, Hidalgo state, Mexico. It is one of the oldest sites in America with evidence of human occupation, having cave paintings of approximately 13,000 years old. At the site, a pyramid of three bodies of Teotihuacan influence stands out, 12 metres (39.3 ft) base and 8 metres (26.2 ft) high, with an altar and a set of cave paintings that date to approximately 13,000 years ago.

(400 - 1000 AD) Huari, or Wari, is an archaeological site located near the town of Quinua, 22 km (13.6 mi) northeast of the city of Ayacucho, in the Ayacucho Region, Peru at an elevation about 2,800 metres (9,186 ft). It was the capital city of the Huari Empire and one of the largest urban settlements in ancient Peru. Buildings are made of stone and mudbrick, and painted in red and white. Many of the structures had residential, administrative or religious purposes.

(1438 - 1530 AD) Huayna Picchu is a mountain in Peru around which the Urubamba River bends. It is located in the Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District. It rises over Machu Picchu, the so-called lost city of the Incas. The Incas built a trail up the side of the Huayna Picchu and built temples and terraces on its top. Huayrapongo is an archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Cajamarca Region, San Miguel Province, Llapa District. The site lies on the mountain Huayrapongo.

(1150 - 1450 AD) Huayuri, also called the Lost City of Huayuri, is a large pre-Columbian archaeological site which flourished from 1150 to 1450 AD in the Late Intermediate Period of Peru. Huayuri is located about 80 km (50 mi) from the Pacific Ocean at an elevation of 500 metres (1,600 ft) in Santa Cruz District of Palpa Province in the Ica Region of Peru. Its prominence was probably dependent upon an climatic phase in which the area received greater precipitation than at earlier and later perio

(1000 - 1530 AD) Huchuy Qosqo is an Incan archaeological site north of Cuzco, Peru. Its name is Quechua for "Little Cuzco." It lies at an elevation of 3,650 metres (11,980 feet), overlooking the Sacred Valley and 3 km (1.9 mi) west and above the town of Lamay at an elevation of 2,920 metres (9,580 ft). Huchuy Qosqo or Kakya Qawani, as it was known by the Incas, was probably established as a royal estate by the Inca Emperor Viracocha about 1420 AD.

(6th c. BC - 6th c. AD) Huckhoe Settlement is an archaeological site in Northumberland, England, near the village of Bolam and about 11 km (7 mi) west of Morpeth. The site shows occupation, in at least four phases, dating from the early Iron Age (6th century BC) to the post-Roman period (6th century AD). It is a scheduled monument. (9th c. BC) Huelva is a municipality of Spain and the capital of the province of Huelva, in the autonomous community of Andalusia. Located in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, it sits between the estuaries of the Odiel and Tinto rivers on the Atlantic coast of the Gulf of Cádiz. (1100 AD) Huerfano Butte is a small rocky butte located on the western flank of the Santa Rita Mountains in southeastern Pima County, Arizona. Huerfano Butte is an important Prehistoric archaeological site. Huerfano Butte and the surrounding area were utilized by the Hohokam as early as circa 1100 AD. (1st ml. BC) Huéscar (Latin: Osca) is a municipality of the province of Granada, Spain. When the Iberian Peninsula was conquered by Rome, Osca was a town of the Turdetani, and incorporated into the Roman province of Hispania Baetica. However, purportedly ancient coins from this town are not genuine. Huichún is an archaeological site in Peru. The site consists of houses, stone tombs (chullpa), deposits (qullqa) and enclosures. Huichún is situated in the village of Cochamarca about 8 km (5 mi) from the town of Obas. It lies in the Huánuco Region, Yarowilca Province, Obas District.

Huichún is an archaeological site in Peru. The site consists of houses, stone tombs (chullpa), deposits (qullqa) and enclosures. Huichún is situated in the village of Cochamarca about 8 km (5 mi) from the town of Obas. It lies in the Huánuco Region, Yarowilca Province, Obas District.

(2nd ml. BC) Huilai Monument Archaeology Park (traditional Chinese: 惠來遺址; simplified Chinese: 惠来遗址; pinyin: Huìlái Yízhǐ) is an archaeological site at Xitun District, Taichung, Taiwan. The site was discovered by Tunghai University student Chen Sheng-ming in 2002. Further investigation revealed the site coverage to be 1.5 square kilometres (0.57 sq mi) and the Taichung City Government declared the area to be a City Archaeological Area. Huillca Raccay is an archaeological site in Peru located in the Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Ollantaytambo District. It is situated southeast of the archaeological site Patallacta above the right bank of the little river Pampa Qhawa, an affluent of the Vilcanota River, near the village Chamana.

Huiñao is a mountain in the Andes of Peru, about 3,645 metres (11,959 ft) high. It lies in the Arequipa Region, La Unión Province, Cotahuasi District. What makes the mountain so special among the much higher mountains surrounding it is that it is situated in the Cotahuasi Canyon and that there are good panoramic views from its top across the Cotahuasi Canyon and the surrounding mountains. (3300 - 3200 BC) The Hulbjerg Passage Grave is a passage grave located at the southern end of the Danish island Langeland, situated on a 15 metre (49 ft) hill south of the ferry harbour Bagenkop. Dating back to 3300 - 3200 BC, it is part of the Neolithic Funnelbeaker culture. The grave consists of a chamber and a separate lateral passageway. This form of grave is predominantly found in Germany and Scandinavia, and to a lesser extent in France and the Netherlands. The rectangular grave chamber is

(3000 BC - 1st c. AD) Humbleton Hill is a hill in Northumberland, England, about 2.4 km (1.5 mi) west of Wooler. It is the location of the Battle of Homildon Hill of 1402 AD, between English and Scottish armies. There is an archaeological site on the summit, with remains of an enclosed settlement of the Neolithic Age and a later Iron Age hillfort. It is a scheduled monument.

(2nd ml. BC - 15th c. AD) Hundatorra is a deserted Medieval village near Hound Tor on Dartmoor, Devon. The site has seen two periods of historic occupation, the first in the Bronze Age from around 1700 - 1200 BC and deserted by 1000 BC, and the reoccupation during the Medieval Warm Period until approximately the 14th century. The village site is around 340 metres (1,100 ft) above sea level, and on a north east-facing slope.

(600 - 400 BC) Hundersingen is a village within the municipality of Herbertingen and is part of the administrative district of Sigmaringen in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The village of Hundersingen is situated on the steep molasse hillside towards the left bank of the Danube and on its adjacent plateau. (2nd c. AD) Hunnum (also known as Onnum, and with the modern name of Halton Chesters) was a Roman fort north of the modern-day village of Halton, Northumberland in North East England. It was the fifth fort on Hadrian's Wall, after Segedunum (Wallsend), Pons Aelius (Newcastle), Condercum and Vindobala. (7th - 4th c. BC) Hunsbury Hill is an Iron Age hill fort 3 km (2 mi) south-west of the centre of the town of Northampton in the county of Northamptonshire. It is probable that defences were built at Hunsbury Hill between the 7th and 4th centuries BC. The deep ditch excavated has survived to the present day. (3rd ml. BC) Huntersquoy Chambered Cairn is a Neolithic chambered cairn located on the island of Eday, in Orkney, Scotland. The monument dates from the 3rd millennium BC and is an Orkney-Cromarty type chambered cairn. Huntersquoy chambered cairn is situated on a gently sloping hill overlooking Calf Sound. (1st ml. BC) Hunter's Tor is a Granite tor located in the parish of Lustleigh, on Dartmoor. It is one of two tors with the same name, the other being in the Teign Gorge. Hunter's Tor is in the Lustleigh Cleave, on the apex of a ridge above the River Bovey. The tor is a natural viewpoint, and there is visibility to Haytor, Bowerman's Nose and Hamel Down. The tor is the location for an Iron Age hill fort, probably due to the views and defensibility of the site. The hill fort was an oval enclosure

(1st ml. BC) Huntsham Castle, Devon, England is an Iron Age Hill fort enclosure near the village of Huntsham, it is located 260 metres (850 ft) above sea level on the edge of the former Parish of Tiverton. The monument includes a slight univallate hillfort situated on a prominent hill overlooking the valleys of two separate tributaries to the River Lowman. (12th - 1st c. BC) A Syrian village. Hosn Suleiman was known as Baetocaece which was famous for its slave market. The town had a temple of Zeus and it is hinted from the naming, that it bears semitic roots derived from Zeus's name. Also known as Baal (Bel) temple, ascribed to the god Baal.

(8th - 2nd c. BC) Hybla Gereatis was an ancient city of Magna Graecia in Sicily, located on the southern slope of Mount Etna, not far from the river Symaethus, in the modern comune of Paternò. There were at least three (and possibly as many as five) cities named "Hybla" in ancient accounts of Sicily which are often confounded with each other, and which it is sometimes very difficult to distinguish. (1700 - 1500 BC) The Hypogeum of Cala Sant Vicenç is a set of caves dating back to the Bronze Age (1700 - 1500 BC), located on the Spanish island of Mallorca. Today, eight caves are visible, though when they were studied by Wilfrid James Hemp, there were fifteen. Some features of the caves are modern (such as the hole at the back of Cave 7). The taula-like statue at the entrance to the site is also modern.

(1700 - 1400 BC) The Hypogeum of Torre del Ram is an archaeological site in Cala en Blanes, Ciutadella de Menorca. It is a Bronze Age funerary hypogeum, which was used as a collective tomb by a family or a small community. Even though it was emptied in later centuries to be reused as a cattle shelter, causing the loss of all information regarding the interred population, grave goods and chronology, its resemblance with other Prehistoric tombs of Menorca dates it to between 1700 and 1400 BC. (1290 - 1224 BC) The Great Hypostyle Hall is located within the Karnak temple complex, in the Precinct of Amon-Re. The structure was built around the 19th Egyptian Dynasty. Its design was initially instituted by Hatshepsut, at the northwest chapel to Amun in the upper terrace of Deir el-Bahri. The name refers to hypostyle architectural pattern. (5th c. BC) Ialysus or Ialysos, also Ialyssus or Ialyssos, or Ielyssus or Ielyssos, was a city of ancient Rhodes. It was one of the three ancient Doric cities in the island, and one of the six towns constituting the Doric hexapolis. It was situated only six stadia (1,110 metres (3,642 ft)) to the south-west of the city of Rhodes, and it would seem that the rise of the latter city was the cause of the decay of Ialysus; for in the time of Strabo it existed only as a village. It runs from the Fosse Way at Bourton on the Water in Gloucestershire  to Templeborough in South Yorkshire. It passes through Alcester, Studley, Redditch, Metchley Fort, Birmingham, Sutton Coldfield, Lichfield, Burton upon Trent and Derby. The Icknield Way is an ancient trackway in southern and eastern England that runs from Norfolk to Wiltshire. It follows the chalk escarpment that includes the Berkshire Downs and Chiltern Hills. It is generally said to be, within Great Britain, one of the oldest roads the route of which can still be traced, being one of the few long-distance trackways to have existed before the Romans occupied the country. (4th - 1st ml. BC) Idaean Cave is a system of caves located on the slopes of Mount Ida on Crete. The deep cave has a single entrance and features stalagmites and stalactites. In antiquity it was a place of worship because it was believed to be the cave where the titan Rhea hid the infant Zeus, to protect him from his father Cronus, who intended to swallow him like others of his progeny. (168 BC) The remains of the ancient Lycian city Idebessos. On site: the necropolis, the acropolis, a Greek theatre, a bath-gymnasium complex, a 5th century church and a small triconch church.

(1st c. AD) Ide is a village in Devon, England, just under 1.6 km (1 mi) south-west of Exeter. The village church is dedicated to the German Saint Ida of Herzfeld and was rebuilt in 1834. The village has two pubs: the Poacher's Inn and the Huntsman Inn. Above Ide on a hilltop is the site of a Roman fortlet or signal station.

(5th c. BC) Idomenae or Idomenai (Ancient Greek: Ἰδομεναί, possibly from Ἰδομενεύς - Idomeneus), was a town of ancient Macedonia. The Tabula Peutingeriana places Idomenae between Stena and Tauriana; 17.7 km (11 mi) from Stena. Sitalces, king of Thrace, on his route from Thrace to Macedonia, crossed Mount Cercine, leaving the Paeones on his right, and the Sinti and Maedi on his left, and descended upon the long river Axius at Idomenae. (250 AD) The Igel Column is a multi-storeyed Roman sandstone column in the municipality of Igel, Trier, Germany, dated to c. 250 AD. The column is the burial monument of the Secundinii cloth merchant family, and was built by two of the family members, Lucius Secundinius Aventinus and Lucius Secundinus Securus. (700 - 550 BC) Igeum-dong is a complex archaeological site located in Igeum-dong, Samcheonpo in Sacheon-si, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea. This Prehistoric archaeological site is important in Korean prehistory because it represents solid evidence that simple chiefdoms formed in as early as the Middle Mumun, some 950 years before the first state-level societies formed in Korea. The settlement is dated by pottery, pit-house types, and an AMS radiocarbon date to the Late Middle Mumun Potte

(900 - 1530 AD) Ihuatzio is a town in Michoacán located 10 km (6 mi) from Pátzcuaro, and founded by the Purépechas. The archaeological zone of Ihuatzio is of great importance. It was used as an astronomical observatory and ceremonial center until the arrival of the conquerors. Although it is small, because the lack of economic resources has allowed archaeologists to rescue only 10% of the area; Its wall and its pyramids dedicated to Curicaueri and Xaratanga stand out.

(2nd ml. BC) Iklaina (Greek: Ίκλαινα) is a historic village in the municipal unit of Pylos, Messenia, Greece. The settlement, which is situated in low hills approximately 10 km (6.2 mi) northeast of Pylos, stands upon the remains of a Late Bronze Age (ca. 1600 - 1100 BC) city. An archaeological site has been surveyed and excavated there by the Athens Archaeological Society and the University of Missouri-St. Louis under the direction of Michael Cosmopoulos. Finds include an early Mycenaean palace

(3rd - 6th c. AD) Illerup Ådal is a river valley and archaeological site located near Skanderborg in East Jutland, Denmark. According to Forte, Professor Oram, and Pedersen, "The Illerup Ådal site is one of twenty-five in Denmark and southern Sweden where weapons were sacrificed." (2nd - 3rd c. AD) An ancient place founded as a summer residence for wealthy citizens of Seleukia. Seven house and temple graves are the main surviving structures, with some being two stories high; the tallest are 7.5 metres (24.6 ft). On the acropolis hill, there are some remains of the ancient city, including a Roman bath house with a mosaic floor showing the sea god and a Greek inscription. There are also the remains of the columns of two Heroa.

(1000 - 1500 AD) Iñaq Uyu is an archaeological site in Bolivia situated on the Isla de la Luna, an island of Lake Titicaca. Iñaq Uyu dates back to around 1000 to 1500 AD. Like the other archaeological sites, Chinkana and Pillkukayna, Iñaq Uyu is located on an island of Lake Titicaca; however, Iñaq Uyu is situated on the Isla de la Luna, rather than the larger Isla Del Sol where Chinkana and Pillkukayna are situated. In 1983 the Pisac National Archeological Park was established to recognize the importance of and to protect the remains of the complex. (1438 - 1530 AD) Incahuasi is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Lima Region, Cañete Province, Lunahuaná District.

(13th - 16th c. AD) An archaeological site of cut-stone structures. The site is an arrangement of carved stones (phalluses) protruding from the earth within a walled rectangular ruin. At the entrance there are two rocks carved of a male member, in addition to 80 similar to the interior of the temple. According to scientific research, the temple corresponds to the Inca period. The site previously consisted of large buildings and was a major center of power.

(2400 BC) Independence Fjord or Independence Sound is a large fjord or sound in the eastern part of northern Greenland. It is about 200 km (120 mi) long and up to 30 km (19 mi) wide. In the area around Independence Fjord there are traces of two paleo-Eskimo cultures that were named Independence I culture and Independence II culture after the fjord. (13th - 16th c. AD) The largest known Inca ruins in Ecuador. Used as an astronomical observatory and for religious functions. The most significant building is the Temple of the Sun, an elliptically shaped building constructed around a large rock. It is constructed in the Inca way without mortar, as are most of the structures in the complex. The stones were carefully chiseled and fashioned to fit together perfectly.
A large rock formation in gneiss. It is composed of some basalt stones covered with symbols and glyphs, some of which are yet to be deciphered.
Ingatambo is an archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Cajamarca Region, Jaén Province, Pomahuaca District.
Inkachaka or Inka Chaka is an archaeological site in Bolivia. It is situated in the Cochabamba Department, Chapare Province, Colomi Municipality.
(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Mach'ay is an Inca archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Huancavelica Region, Tayacaja Province, Ñahuimpuquio District.

Inka Murata is an archaeological site in the Altiplano of Bolivia. It is located in the Oruro Department, Litoral Province, Escara Municipality, in the community of Escara. The site with the adjacent burial towers was declared a National Historical Monument in 2008.

(1438 - 1530 AD) Inkapintay is an Inca archaeological site in Peru with a rock painting. It is situated in the Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Ollantaytambo District, near Ollantaytambo. The figure which draws the attention possibly depicts a noble person.
Inka Raqay is an archaeological site in Bolivia. It is located in the Cochabamba Department, Quillacollo Province, Sipe Sipe Municipality, near the community of Linku.

(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Raqay is a small Inca archaeological complex in Peru. It lies in the Apurímac Region, Abancay Province, Cachora District. Inka Raqay is situated at a height of 3,590 metres (11,778 ft) on the northern slope of Inka Wasi south of the archaeological site of Choquequirao, above the Apurímac River.
(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Raqay is an Inca archaeological site in the Ayacucho Region in Peru. It is located in the Huanta Province, Iguain District, on top of the mountain named Allqu Willka.
(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Tampu is an Inca archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Cusco Region, La Convención Province, Huayopata District, at a height of about 2,127 metres (6,978 ft).

(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Tampu is an Inca archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Cusco Region, La Convención Province, Vilcabamba District. The archaeological group is situated on top of a mountain named Inka Tampu (Inka Tambo).

Inka Tunuwiri is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Puno Region, Puno Province, between the districts Chucuito and Puno, southeast of the village Ichu. Inka Tunuwiri was declared a National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) of Peru by the National Institute of Culture.
(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Wasi is an Inca archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Ayacucho Region, Parinacochas Province, Pullo District.

(1438 - 1530 AD) Inka Wasi, Huancavelica is an archaeological site in the Huancavelica Region in Peru. The Inca palace is considered one of the most important monuments of the Huancavelica Region. Inka Wasi is located in the Huaytará Province, Huaytará District, about 25 km (16 mi) from Huaytará. It is situated at a height of 3,804 metres (12,480 ft).
(1438 - 1530 AD) Inkilltambo is an archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Cusco Region, Cusco Province, San Sebastián District.

(2500 - 1000 BC) Innisidgen is the site of two Bronze Age entrance graves on the island of St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly. The two burial monuments, (Upper and Lower Innisidgen) lie on a steep slope of Innisidgen Hill overlooking Crow Sound with a view towards the Eastern Isles. (1438 - 1530 AD) The Intihuatana Archaeological Complex is an Inca archaeological site. The complex was considered a residential zone and a retreat for the Inca elite. The site is made up of a series of buildings. Among others you’ll find a palace, a tower, and the baths of the Inca, featuring a carved stone with 13 angles.

(1438 - 1530 AD) An ancient Inca ritual stone. Also known as the “Solar Clock”,  it is a piece carved in stone in the shape of a polygon. It has a large base and at the top there is a protrusion, like a pillar, that has a height of approximately 2 metres (6.5 ft), it was delicately sculpted, with mathematically defined cuts that aligns with the cardinal points. According to historians it was used to record the passage of time and assist in the control of agricultural cycles.

Intikancha, Puno is a mountain with an archaeological site of the same name in the Andes of Peru, about 4,400 metres (14,436 ft) elevation. It is located in the Puno Region, Lampa Province, Nicasio District, and in the San Román Province, Juliaca District.

Intini Uyu Pata is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Puno Region, Yunguyo Province, between the districts Ollaraya and Unicachi, at a height of about 3,867 metres (12,687 ft). The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) of Peru by the National Institute of Culture.

Intipanawin is an archaeological site and the name of a mountain with rock paintings in Peru. It is situated in the Ancash Region, Bolognesi Province, Pacllon District, at a height of about 3,569 metres (11,709 ft). Beside the painting of the eye of the sun there are also paintings of llamas nearby which draw the attention.

Inti Punku is an archaeological site in the Cusco Region of Peru that was once a fortress of the sacred city, Machu Picchu. It is now also the name of the final section of the Incan Trail between the Sun Gate complex and the city of Machu Picchu. It was believed that the steps were a control gate for those who enter and exited the Sanctuary. It is one of the most important archaeological constructions around the Machu Picchu site. Inti Watana is an archaeological site in Peru. It lies in the Cusco Region, Calca Province, Pisac District.

Intiyuq K'uchu is an archaeological site in Peru with rock paintings. It is located in the Cusco Region, Calca Province, Lamay District. Intiyuq K'uchu is situated at a height of about 3,800 metres (12,467 ft).

According to ancient Greek mythology, Aeson was the rightful king of Iolcus, but his half-brother Pelias usurped the throne. (1200 - 300 BC) The Ipf is a mostly treeless mountain, 668 metres (2,192 ft) high, near Bopfingen, Ostalbkreis, Baden-Württemberg, Germany, with a Prehistoric Hill Fort on its top. Iskuqucha is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Junín Region, Yauli Province, La Oroya District.

(100 - 1520 AD) Isla de Sacrificios is a Mexican island located in the Gulf of Mexico, close to the port of Veracruz. (500 - 1400 AD) Isla Palenque is located off the western Pacific shore of Panama, near the border of Costa Rica, in the Gulf of Chiriquí. (350 BC -1200 AD) Topoxte is a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in the Petén Basin in northern Guatemala with a long occupational history dating as far back as the Middle Preclassic. As the capital of the Kowoj Maya, it was the largest of the few Postclassic Mesoamerican sites in the area. The principal ruins of the city are spread over three islands: Topoxte, Cante and Paxte, in the southwest of Yaxha Lake, of which Topoxte is the largest.

(200 - 650 AD) Ismantorp Fortress is the ruins of a ringfort located on Öland Island in Sweden. One of approximately 20 known ringforts located on Öland, Ismantorp was constructed during the Migration Period. Isog is an archaeological site in Peru. It is situated in the Huánuco Region, Huamalíes Province, Tantamayo District. Isog lies on the northern slope of the mountain Susupillo, which is also the name of the archaeological site south of Isog.

(7th c. BC) Isthmia is an ancient sanctuary of Poseidon and important archaeological site and museum located on the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece. (78,000 BC) The Isturitz and Oxocelhaya Caves are an important Paleolithic site where a Neanderthal mandible was found, as well as later modern human finds associated with the Aurignacian, Solutrean and Magdalenian. (2nd - 4th c. AD) The Iturranduz Dam was a Roman buttress dam in Navarra, Spain. It consisted of two dams, one dating to the 2nd, the other to the 3rd or 4th century AD.

(1st ml. BC) Ivinghoe is a village and civil parish in east Buckinghamshire, England, close to the borders with Hertfordshire and Bedfordshire. (3rd ml. BC) Jannusan Burial Mound Field is a mound field located in Northern Governorate, Bahrain. It is dating back to Dilmun period in 3rd millennium BC. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019 as part of Dilmun Burial Mounds.

(3rd c. BC) Justinianopolis was a town of ancient Epirus and of Illyricum, the successor settlement to Hadrianopolis that was repaired and moved by Justinian I. It was one of the cities of the government of old Epirus. The bishop's see that had been established at Hadrianopolis was translated to Dryinopolis rather than to Justinianopolis. Its site is located near Bregu i Melanit, Nepravishtë, in Albania.

(3rd c. BC) Juvanum or Jovanum was one of the chief cities of the Caraceni, a tribe of Samnites, the ruins of which are located in the communes of Montenerodomo and Torricella Peligna, in the province of Chieti in the Abruzzo region of Italy. It is an archaeological site, and the ruins encompass a forum, temple, and basilica, and remains of the Roman conquest during the Social War after which youths were settled at the site (whence, in some views, its Latin name). The site is open to the public.

(7th - 11th c. AD) Kabáh is a Maya archaeological site located in the municipality of Santa Elena, State of Yucatán, Mexico, southeast of Uxmal that is part of the so-called Puuc route. The area was already inhabited, in the middle of the 3rd century BC. Most of the architecture visible today was built in the 7th and 11th centuries. Kabah was abandoned, or at least no more ceremonial centers were built, several centuries before the Spanish conquistadores arrived in Yucatán. An elevated pedestria
(1st - 2nd c. AD) A group of seven Buddhist caves carved out on the mountain. The architecture of the caves shows vihara style construction influenced by Buddhist architecture.

(5th c. BC - 7th c. AD) A town of ancient Lycia. Extensive remains today include a stadium, a theatre, baths, walls, agora and several temples. Mostly the south parts of the wall still remain. Polygonal city walls from the Hellenistic Period formed retaining walls of the ancient theatre and show a high quality workmanship. Most of the remaining ruins in Cadianda belongs to the Roman Period. The necropolis has been plundered and partly destroyed. The tombs close to the city have a vaulted form, r

(1601 - 1874 AD) Constructed in 1601 by Matsudaira Iehisa, head of the Shimazu clan and the first daimyō of the Satsuma Domain, during the early Edo period. The castle is notable for the small scale and fairly poor quality as a main castle of one of the richest domains in Japan. The castle was destroyed in a fire in 1874 and not rebuilt, and is now only ruins with only the castle's moats and stone walls remaining.

(1st - 2nd c. AD) The remains of a castle built by the Commagene civilization. On site are: the bazaar, mosque, dungeon, and waterways. Kahta Castle is one of the best preserved historical castles in Türkiye.

(4th c. AD) Kahu-Jo-Darro is an ancient Buddhist stupa found at the Mirpurkhas archaeological site in Sindh, Pakistan. The site is spread over 12 hectares (30 acres). Excavations completed before 1910 revealed this large brick-based stupa and numerous terracotta reliefs now displayed in major world museums. (30 BC) The Temple of Kalabsha is an ancient Egyptian temple that was originally located at Bab al-Kalabsha (Gate of Kalabsha), approximately 50 km (31 mi) south of Aswan. In the 1960s the temple was relocated under the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979, along with other outstanding examples of Nubian architecture including Abu Simbel and Amada. (9th c. BC) Beška (Serbian Cyrillic: Бешка) is a village in Serbia. It is situated in the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina, in the region of Syrmia (Syrmia District), in Inđija municipality. Roman tombs with rich decorative paintings dating back to the third or the fourth century were discovered in Beška. It was first mentioned in 1564. During Ottoman rule (16th - 17th century) the village of Beška was populated by Serbs. During Habsburg rule, ethnic Germans settled there. Following World War II

(2nd - 1st ml. BC) Kalapodi is a modern Greek village in the Lokroi municipality, Phthiotis, Central Greece. Lokroi straddles the pass leading over the low mountains between the Bay of Atalantis in the Gulf of Euboea to the plains of Boeotia north of Lake Copais. The road is often termed the Atalanti-Livadeia. The community of Atalanti, the chief deme of Lokroi, overlooks the Bay of Atalantis, while Livadeia is the current capital of Voiotia. (1st c. AD) Kalawan is the name of an archaeological site in the area of Taxila in Pakistan, where it is one of the largest Buddhist establishment. It is located about 2 km (1.2 mi) from the Dharmarajika stupa. Kalawan has a vihara monastery, which is the largest in northern India. An inscription, recording the enshrinement of relics as a gift to the Sarvastivadin School, was found in a chaitya hall mentioning the date of "the 134th year of Azes," which corresponds to 77 AD. BC) Kale-Krševica is an archaeological site in Serbia, dating back mainly to the Late Classical and Early Hellenistic periods. It holds the remains of the northernmost Ancient Macedonian city so far discovered. The site is located in the hills of Krševica overlooking Bujanovac and Vranje, to the south of Ristovac in southern Serbia. Kaljaja is an archaeological site, which is located southeast of the village of Balovac, in municipality of Podujevo. Fortification of an irregular trapezoid shape, with the remains of the ramparts was discovered. Remains follow the terrain configuration. Construction technique was cut stone and brick. Kaljaja is an archaeological site, which is located in Teneš Do on the hill Kaljaja (municipality of Pristina) in Kosovo. Remains of fortress walls and buildings were uncovered at the site. Remains of bricks were also found. Based on the traces found on the slope hill Kaljaj it is assumed that the village was burnt. Fragments of ceramics were discovered. (9 AD) Kalkriese is a village now administratively part of the city of Bramsche in the district of Osnabrück, Lower Saxony, Germany. It is on the northern slope of the Wiehen Hills, a ridge-like range of hills, north of Osnabrück. The Kalkrieser Berg or Schmittenhöhe, a hill with a height of 157 metres (515 ft), is considered by archaeologists to be the likely site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest. (9 AD) The Kalkrieser Berg (also called the Schmittenhöhe) is a hill, 157 metres (515 ft), between the villages of Venne and Engter, in the district of Osnabrück. The Kalkrieser Berg is a northern bulge of the Wiehen Hills. To the north is the great bog of Großes Moor at a height of about 47 metres (154 ft) above sea level (NHN), the Mittelland Canal, built in the 20th century, and the Bramsche parish of Kalkriese. K'allapayuq Urqu is an archaeological site in the Ayacucho Region in Peru on top of a mountain of the same name. The Chanka site lies in the La Mar Province, Anco District, between the communities of Uskhuqucha (Husjucocha, Osqoqocha, Uscoqocha) and Anchiway (Anchihuay). It is situated at a height of about 3,935 metres (12,910 ft).

(4th - 1st c. BC) Kalos Limen (Ancient Greek: Καλός Λιμήν, lit. 'Charming Harbor'; Ukrainian: Калос-Лімен) is an ancient Greek colony on the east coast of the Crimean Peninsula that existed from 4th to 1st centuries BC. Kalos Limen was established by Ionian settlers in 4th century BC. The city was 4 hectares (9.9 acres) in size and was surrounded by walls. Kalos Limen was divided into sections, and a tower was located in the center of each. By the end of 4th century BC, the city belonged to Cher

(4th - 2nd ml. BC) Kamares is a village in south-central Crete, Greece. It is the location of an archaeological site of a Minoan sacred cave. The sacred cave at Kamares is slightly offset from a saddle in the Psiloriti Range virtually aligned with the location of nearby Phaistos. Some of the best examples of Middle Minoan pottery have been recovered from the Kamares cave. (Unknown) A mysterious megalith carved to resemble a turtle.

(3000 - 700 BC) The Kamenica Tumulus is an archaeological site in Kamenicë, Korçë County, Albania. The site includes a museum dedicated to the prehistory of Albania and of the surrounding region. Excavations show that the Tumulus of Kamenica represents the largest burial monument of its kind in relation to 200 tumuli excavated in Albania and neighboring Balkan countries. A Megalithic site and protected nature reserve.

(4th - 2nd ml. BC) Kamilari is a village on the island of Crete, Greece. There is an archaeological site of an ancient Minoan cemetery nearby. Kamilari is built atop three hills: Ovgora, meaning "good view" is the highest one with an altitude of 110 metres (360.8 ft), Goulas is the one with the old school and the Hellenistic findings on top and Alevrota, reachable from the village exit in direction of Sivas. (1500 BC - 1200 AD) Kaminaljuyu is a Pre-Columbian site of the Maya civilization located in Guatemala City. Primarily occupied from 1500 BC to 1200 AD, it has been described as one of the greatest archaeological sites in the New World, although the extant remains are distinctly unimpressive. Debate continues about its size, integration, and role in the surrounding Valley of Guatemala and the Southern Maya area.

(20th c. BC - 17th c. AD) Kamyana Mohyla (Ukrainian: Кам'яна Могила, romanized: Kamiana Mohyla, lit. 'stone grave') is an archaeological site in the Molochna River (lit. 'milk river') valley, about 1.6 km (1 mi) from the village of Terpinnia, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine. Petroglyphs of Kamyana Mohyla are dated from Upper Paleolithic (Kukrek culture) to Medieval, with Stone Age depictions subjected to most archaeological interest. Kanamarka is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Cusco Region, Espinar Province, Alto Pichigua District.
(1st - 10th c. AD) A complex of caves and rock-cut monuments, cut into a massive basalt outcrop.

(1000 AD) Kanichi is an archaeological site in Peru. Kanichi lies in the Ayacucho Region, Lucanas Province, Carmen Salcedo District. The archaeological complex was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures.  The complex includes a variety of buildings including Chullpas, religious and ceremonial buildings, service centers, and a water system of wells and springs.

(2nd c. AD) The Kanishka Stupa was a monumental stupa established by the Kushan king Kanishka during the 2nd century in today's Shaji-ki-Dheri on the outskirts of Peshawar, Pakistan. The location was re-identified in 2011. It is located outside the Gunj Gate of the old Walled City of Peshawar and is called Akhunabad. The stupa was built during the Kushan era to house Buddhist relics, and was among the tallest buildings in the ancient world. The stupa is also famous for its Buddhist relics, which

(3rd c. BC) Kanlı Divane in an ancient city settlement built around a large natural depression called the Kanlı Divane Pothole. In the main settlement there are basilicas made of cut stone, streets, rock tombs and cisterns. There is a tower in the southwest of the settlement. Three necropolises have been identified around the city.
The remains of the monastery of Karabelli Sion.
(3rd - 7th c. AD) Karabel Kilisesi, located in Çağman, Demre/Antalya, Türkiye, are the remains of an ancient Byzantine church.
(3rd c. BC - 4th c. AD) The site of an ancient Hellenistic settlement.

(4th c. BC) Karaburma (Serbian Cyrillic: Карабурма) is an urban neighbourhood of the municipality of Palilula, Belgrade, Serbia. The name, Karaburma, is Turkish for 'black ring' which is supposed to mean that the area was forbidden, that is, it should be avoided by people. However, this may be an example of folk etymology as the old Ottoman and Austrian maps name the area Kajaburun (Kaya-burun) which is Turkish for rocky headland. (9th ml. BC) An archaeological site located close to Göbekli Tepe where archaeologists have uncovered T-shaped pillars and animorphic figures. It is part of the Göbeklitepe Culture and Karahantepe Excavations project. It is part of a region of similar sites now being uncovered known as the Taş Tepeler.

An archaeological site. The settlement dates back to Hellenistic age but it was rebuilt and inhabited during the Roman and early Byzantine ages. It was probably abandoned during the Arab/Byzantine wars. There are many houses and seven of them are in relatively good condition. Four of them are one-storey and three of them are two-storey houses constructed of limestone. There are also, basilicas, a tetrapylon, cisterns, and a partially unearthed Roman road.

(30 - 20 BC) A funerary monument-a hierothesion-for Queen Isias and Princesses Antiochis and Aka I of Commagene. The monument is a column topped by an eagle, and it has Greek honorific inscriptions on the external faces of the two drums of the central column of the northeast.

(2nd c. BC)) The remains of an ancient fortress built by the Macedonian Seleucids. The fortress has not yet been developed for tourism. The ascent over the pathless rock is very steep, difficult and not without danger. It is therefore strongly recommended to be guided by locals from the surrounding villages.
An open-air museum situated in the ruins of an ancient fortification.

(4th - 1st c. BC) Karchaghbyur is a village in the Vardenis Municipality of the Gegharkunik province of Armenia. The village was previously known as Gedakbulag. A walled settlement close to Karchaghbyur which was abandoned in the 1st century BC, of the Persian or Hellenistic period, is being excavated.

(1900 - 1600 BC) Karfi is an archaeological site high up in the Dikti Mountains in eastern Crete, Greece. The ancient name of the site is unknown; "Karfi" ("the nail") is a local toponym for the prominent knob of limestone that marks the peak of the site, especially when viewed from the north. (2nd c. BC - 5th c. AD) A complex of ancient Buddhist Indian rock-cut caves associated with the Mahāsāṃghika sect of Buddhism. The Karla cave complex is built into a rocky hillside around 60 km (37.3 mi) from Pune, with large windows cut into the rock to light the cave interiors.

(1971 - 30 BC) The Karnak Temple Complex, commonly known as Karnak, comprises a vast mix of decayed temples, pylons, chapels, and other buildings near Luxor, Egypt. Construction at the complex began during the reign of Senusret I (rgn 1971 - 1926 BC) in the Middle Kingdom (around 2000 - 1700 BC) and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom (305 - 30 BC), although most of the extant buildings date from the New Kingdom. (7th c. BC) Karpasia also known as Karpasion (sometimes mistaken for Karpathos), was an ancient town in Cyprus, situated in the northern shore of the Karpas Peninsula, at a distance of 3 km (1.8 mi) from the modern town of Rizokarpaso. According to tradition, it was founded by the Phoenician king Pygmalion of Tyre. It had a harbour, whose moles remain visible to this day. According to archaeological evidence, the earliest possible date for the foundation of the town is the 7th century BC. It was

(8000 BC) Karta, known since 1802 as Kangaroo Island, South Australia, is the location of an archaeological large-stone-tool production site, which was active probably more than 10,000 years ago. Kartan culture archaeology presents a puzzle, according to historians. Archaeologist Ronald Lampert: "The problem had all the characteristics of a classic mystery story: a large offshore island without people [today], separated, nearly 10,000 years ago, yet with abundant evidence of human population."

(4th - 9th c. AD) The Kashmir Smast caves, also called Kashmir Smats, are a series of natural limestone caves, artificially expanded from the Kushan to the Shahi periods, situated in the Babuzai Sakrah mountains in the Katlang Valley Mardan in Northern Pakistan. (1st c. AD) An ancient Roman settlement known as Cillium. West of the main city of Kasserine lay the remains of the ancient Roman city. On site are: a large ancient theatre carved out of the hillside, a triumphal arch, and several fallen columns. Slightly further away from the rest of the ancient ruins, is the Mausoleum of the Flavii, a large three-story tower-mausoleum.

(4th c. BC) The Kasta Tomb, also known as the Amphipolis Tomb, is the largest ancient tumulus (burial mound) ever discovered in Greece, and by comparison dwarfs that of Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, in Vergina. It is an ancient Macedonian tomb of the last quarter of the 4th century BC, and is enclosed in the Kasta mound near the ancient city of Amphipolis, Central Macedonia, in northern Greece. (2000 BC) Kastelli Giant's Church is a prehistoric stone enclosure situated near Pattijoki in the North Ostrobothnia region of Finland. It is one of the largest of forty such "Giant's Churches" to be found in this region of Finland. It dates to around 2000 BC. The Giant's Church at Kastelli is a rectangular stone enclosure measuring around 60 by 35 metres(197 by 115 ft). The walls are 7 metres (23 ft) wide and survive to a height of 2 metres (6.5 ft). (8000 BC) Kastros is an early Neolithic settlement in Cyprus. It lies at the north-easternmost tip of the Karpasia Peninsula (Cape Apostolos Andreas), about 4 km (2.5 mi) north of Apostolos Andreas Monastery. The settlement is situated on a little plateau at the steep flank of the limestone promontory, about halfway between the main plateau of the peninsula and the sea in a very inaccessible situation. (1st ml. BC) Katalymata ton Plakoton is an archaeological site in the vicinity of Akrotiri, on the island of Cyprus. The archaeological site contained a complex of two religious temples, wholly approximately 100 metre (328 ft) in length. The first temple consists of a three-aisled basilica with a transverse aisle, and is 36 metres (118 ft) wide and 29 metres (95 ft) long. (4th c. AD) Katzenberg Hillfort is a Roman refuge fort near Mayen in Germany dating to the 4th century. The fortification on the Katzenberg hill was built around 300 AD after the Roman limes had been overrun and Germanic tribes had invaded and plundered the Roman Empire (the so-called Limesfall). The inhabitants of the Roman vicus, which was located on the site of the present-day town of Mayen, could escape to the fort in time of danger. (10th c. BC - 15th c. AD) The remains of a city of ancient Caria. The main sights at the archaeological site itself are: the acropolis fortified with Byzantine walls, and a smaller fortification nearby, called Heraklion, the theatre with a capacity of 5,000 guests, the palaestra with its Roman baths, a wind measuring platform, a domed Byzantine basilica, the port agora, the stoa and the nymphaeum. Situated on a steep and rocky peak at an elevation of 713 metres (2,339 ft) above sea level in the northern foothills of the Thripti Mountains, the site overlooks the Gulf of Mirabello and the northern Isthmus of Ierapetra. “Kastro” (“Citadel“ or “Castle”) is a loca

It is situated in the northern foothills of the Thripti Mountains overlooking the Gulf of Mirabello, at an elevation of 427 metres (1,401 ft) above sea level. Ancient rock tombs built during the Hellenistic period.

The site consists of two areas, the north complex and the south complex. As of 2013, survey and excavations have located 90 structures, located in 8 groups. Standing in a farmer's field in remote central Tunisia are the mysterious ruined stone walls of Kbor Klib. No one knows who built the structure or why: it has no inscriptions and few decorative elements. At 45 metres (147.6 ft) long, Kbor Klib is constructed of three platforms joined together by a wall, now only about 6 metres (19.6 ft) tall but thought to have once been much higher.

(12th c. BC) Keal Cotes, forming part of West Keal parish, is a small linear village in East Lindsey district of Lincolnshire, England. It is situated on the A16 road, 1.6 km (1 mi) south from West Keal and 1.6 km (1 mi) north from Stickford. The remains of a substantial Roman villa or high status Romano-British farmhouse, the only one found in Lincolnshire, are in a large field at the south end of the village. The name of the village is occasionally spelt on some maps as "Keal Coates". The area

(4th - 1st ml. BC) Kealkill Stone Circle is a Bronze Age axial five-stone circle located just outside the village of Kealkill, County Cork in southwest Ireland. This well-known stone circle is set on the slopes of Maughanclea Hill at 120 - 150 metres (400 - 500 ft) overlooking Bantry Bay on ground that would have been suitable for cultivation. (6th c. BC) Kechries (Greek: Κεχριές) is a village in the municipality of Corinth in Corinthia in Greece, part of the community of Xylokeriza. It takes its name from the ancient port town Kenchreai or Cenchreae (Ancient Greek: Κεγχρεαί), which was situated at the same location. Kechries is located about 8 km (5 mi) southeast of modern Corinth and 4 km (2.5 mi) southwest of Isthmia, at the eastern end of the Corinth Canal. (10,000 BC) The Keilor Archaeological Site was among the first places to demonstrate the antiquity of Aboriginal occupation of Australia when a cranium, unearthed in 1940, was found to be nearly 15,000 years old. Subsequent investigations of Pleistocene alluvial terraces revealed hearths about 29,000 years BC, making Keilor one of the earliest sites of human habitation in Australia. Remains of megafauna suggest a possible association with Aboriginal hunting. The site is located at the confluence

(10th c. BC) Founded by the Lycians, Kekova Island is an uninhabitated long and narrow island, with a coast dotted with archaeological remains. In addition to the flooded city buildings in the north, there is a port, two docks, three churches, two chapels, a bath, two towers/lighthouses, plus four production workshops. There are also Lycian sarcophagi in the sea.

(400 - 100 BC) Kelly Rounds, or Castle Killibury is an Iron Age hill fort in Cornwall, England, United Kingdom. It is situated beside the A39 trunk road approximately 3.2 km (2 mi) east of Wadebridge. The site is north of the village of St Mabyn, approximately 300 metres (984 ft) east of Three Holes Cross on the border of the parish of Egloshayle. (1st ml. BC) Kelsborrow Castle is an Iron Age hill fort in Cheshire, northern England. It is one of only seven hill forts in the county of Cheshire and was probably in use for only a short time. In the 19th century, a bronze palstave was recovered from the site. It is protected as a Scheduled Ancient Monument. (1st ml. BC) Kelsey Head is a coastal Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and headland in north Cornwall, England, United Kingdom, noted for its biological interest. The site contains an Iron Age hill fort. The headland is the site of earthwork remains of a 170 by 160 metre (560 by 520 ft) cliff castle, dated to the Iron Age. But there is evidence of earlier habitation on the site, of Mesolithic and Neolithic periods, through the discovery of flint flakes not related to the cliff castle.

(3000 BC) Kempraten-Lenggis is a village (Kirchdorf) within the municipality of Rapperswil-Jona, Wahlkreis (constituency) of See-Gaster in the canton of St. Gallen in Switzerland. The remains of the Gallo-Roman settlement Centum Prata are one of the most important archaeological sites in the canton of St. Gallen; Centrum Prata is located at the so-called Kempratnerbucht, in Rapperswil and Busskirch on Zürichsee lake shore. Settlements in the region of Rapperswil-Jona date back at least 5,000 yea

(1600 - 1350 BC) Kemune (thought to be the ancient city of Zakhiku) is an archaeological site discovered during a low water level in the reservoir of the Mosul Dam in the Nineveh Governorate, part of the Kurdistan region of Iraq in 2013. The Mitanni era city was destroyed by an earthquake around 1350 BC. The site held a palace constructed on the banks of the Tigris River during the days of the Mitanni Empire rule over Assyria. (1438 - 1530 AD) Kenko, or Quenko, is an Inca archaeological site in the Sacred Valley of Peru located in the Cusco Region consisting of an ancient maze. The maze, located at 3,800 metres (12,467 ft) above sea level, is a huge rocky complex that resembles a big maze for its zigzagging structures. It is composed of two places, Kenko Grande, where there are: The amphitheatre, the carved stone, the solar clock, the Temple of The Monkeys, the zigzagging canals, and the underground chamber. Kenko, Qenqo or Q'inq'u, Puno is an archaeological site in Peru. It is located in the Puno Region, Puno Province, Acora District, at an elevation of about 4,000 metres (13,000 ft). The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) of Peru by the National Institute of Culture.

(2200 BC) Kennet Avenue or West Kennet Avenue is a Prehistoric site in the English county of Wiltshire. It was an avenue of two parallel lines of stones 25 metres (82 ft) wide and 2.5 km (1.5 mi) in length, which ran between the Neolithic sites of Avebury and The Sanctuary. Excavations by Stuart Piggott and Alexander Keiller in the 1930s indicated that around 100 pairs of standing stones had lined the avenue, dated to around 2200 BC from finds of Beaker burials beneath some of them.
